discovery: The optical lattice clock: magic-wavelength trapping of neutral atoms enabling optical frequency measurement at the 10^-18 level and beyond

nominees.name: Hidetoshi Katori
nominees.affiliation: University of Tokyo and RIKEN, Japan

nominees.name: Jun Ye
nominees.affiliation: JILA, NIST and University of Colorado Boulder, USA

subfield: Atomic, molecular and optical physics; precision measurement and metrology
motivation: Katori proposed and first demonstrated trapping neutral atoms in an optical lattice at a 'magic' wavelength, where the light shifts of both clock states cancel. This lets thousands of atoms be interrogated at once, with no motional or trap perturbation. Ye turned the concept into the world's most precise and accurate clocks. He did it through ultrastable lasers, femtosecond-comb-based comparisons, and control of many-body interactions using a degenerate Fermi gas. Together, they improved timekeeping by more than two orders of magnitude beyond caesium standards, reaching uncertainties near 10^-18 and below. Lattice clocks now resolve the gravitational redshift over millimetre height differences. They also test the variation of fundamental constants, probe for dark matter, and are driving the redefinition of the SI second. This is metrology-grade optical physics that has become shared infrastructure and changed what physics can measure.
